During cell differentiation, there typically exists a drastic and sudden shift called cell fate decision-making or bifurcation. Revealing such critical phenomena can provide deeper insights into the fundamental mechanisms that govern the complex intricacies of living organisms. However, many conventional statistical methods fail to predict the specific types of critical transitions and accurately infer cell fate dynamics from single-cell RNA sequencing data. To address this challenge, we develop FatePredictor, a novel computational framework grounded in bifurcation theory and optimal transport theory, to predict cell fate bifurcation based on locally observed information of single-cell data. Specifically, the proposed FatePredictor employs a dynamic unbalanced optimal transport method to reconstruct dynamic cell trajectories, based on which an ensemble deep learning model is utilized to predict the type of dynamics involved in a cell fate bifurcation during cellular processes. The applications on both simulated and real single-cell data demonstrate that FatePredictor serves as a user-friendly and powerful tool for predicting bifurcations of complex biological systems and unveiling intricate cellular trajectories, with higher accuracy compared with many existing methods. Additionally, our FatePredictor has the capacity to pinpoint key genes and pathways related to significant cellular processes.
FatePredictor employs dynamic unbalanced optimal transport method to reconstruct dynamic cell trajectories.

To address the aforementioned challenges, based on optimal transport theory, bifurcation theory, and DL, a novel computational framework called FatePredictor, is developed to reconstruct dynamic trajectories of cellular systems and predict cell fate decision-making using the local observed information of single-cell data. Specifically, a dynamic unbalanced optimal transport method26 is applied to reconstruct dynamic cell trajectories based solely on the local segments of single-cell data, providing latent space representations with clear temporal relationships (Figure 1A). Subsequently, an ensemble DL model is proposed to capture the dynamics of cell fate bifurcation and effectively differentiate between the various types of bifurcations that occur in dynamic cell trajectories (Figure 1B). In this study, two simulated datasets and four real single-cell datasets are employed to showcase the performance of our FatePredictor. The results indicate that our model not only facilitates the identification of specific cell state transitions but also classifies the types of these critical changes, shedding light on the properties of the new state in the system. Specifically, like the concept of early-warning signals for critical states preceding observable phenotypic shifts in dynamical systems, our model can signal a cell fate decision prior to overt phenotypic divergence. For instance, in the human embryonic stem cell (hESC) dataset,27 where a cell fate bifurcation is known to occur between pseudotime 1–2 (24 h) and subsequent stages (36, 72, and 96 h), FatePredictor precisely identifies a Pitchfork bifurcation at pseudotime point 2. When applied to the induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) dataset,28 where a fate decision-making event occurs after the pseudotime 4–6 (2.5–3 days), FatePredictor detects a fold bifurcation at pseudotime point 6, providing a predictive signal at the onset of lineage bifurcation. Furthermore, compared with existing methods for bifurcation prediction, our proposed FatePredictor demonstrates superior performance in predicting cell fate decision-making. Besides, FatePredictor can effectively pinpoint specific gene sets responsible for triggering the bifurcation process, along with the pathways involved in critical cellular processes.

The second part accounts for the deviation of the trajectory from the original, comprising the short-term reconstruction error Rti,ti+1 and long-term reconstruction error Rt1,ti+1. The v and g defined in Equation 22 can be simulated and obtained using two neural networks with identical architectures, each consisting of a fully connected layer and a tanh activation function.33 Overall, by utilizing the dynamic unbalanced optimal transport method, the velocity, trajectory, and growth of cells are effectively recovered based on gene expression and cell population dynamics. The resulting trajectories can act as a latent space representation of the bifurcation dynamics in single-cell data, serving as the input for FatePredictor.

To evaluate the performance of FatePredictor on a real-world dataset, we apply it to chick heart dataset obtained from spontaneously beating chicken heart cell aggregates.40,41 In this dataset, the inter-beat intervals between heartbeats reveal the occurrence of Pd bifurcations following drug administration, which is also observed in the progression of sudden cardiac death. Consequently, the ability to accurately predict these bifurcations at early stages is crucial for the prevention and management of heart disease. In this study, we assess the efficacy of FatePredictor using two bifurcating datasets and one non-bifurcation dataset, each obtained from the chick heart dataset. As shown in Figures 3A–3C, FatePredictor successfully predicts Pd bifurcations in bifurcating data and accurately identifies non-bifurcation data as non-bifurcation (Null), consistent with the observations from the original experiment.40,41 From the perspective of EWSs, including variance and autocorrelation, an increasing trend in variance and a decreasing trend in autocorrelation are observed as precursors to the bifurcation, aligning with theoretical analyses of traditional detection methods prior to Pd bifurcations in dynamical systems.42 However, these indicators exhibit poor performance on non-bifurcation data, as fluctuating trends in both autocorrelation and variance can still occur, potentially leading to false positives. In addition, it can be seen from Figures 3D and 3E and Table 1 that FatePredictor achieves the highest AUC score of 0.96, and performs better than conventional methods such as DL,23 variance, autocorrelation, sample entropy (SE),17 and Kolmogorov complexity (KC)17 in every scenario (see section E of supplemental information for the detailed comparison process). Therefore, FatePredictor can more effectively and accurately predict Pd bifurcations, thereby providing valuable insights for preventing the harmful bifurcations associated with sudden cardiac death.

To demonstrate the ability of FatePredictor in predicting cell fate decisions along dynamic cellular trajectories, we applied it to a time-series scRNA-seq dataset derived from the A549 carcinoma cell line, treated with TGFB1 to induce epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT).43 This dataset consists of cells collected at various time points, with each culture initialized with a uniform cell density, thereby enabling the cell counts at each time point to precisely reflect the population dynamics. As shown in Figure 4A, we utilized a dynamic unbalanced optimal transport method (presented in the materials and methods) to reconstruct the dynamic cell trajectories and population growth patterns based on the global segments of the EMT dataset. The inferred temporal trajectory reveals that epithelial cells initially differentiate into an intermediate state, ultimately progressing to a mesenchymal state. Additionally, we assess the synergistic effects and regulatory relationships of the latent space representations derived from the autoencoder (AE) to cellular proliferation across the differentiation continuum (Figure 4B), uncovering that the dimension with the largest variance AE-1 is the primary dimension capturing bifurcation information and is consequently selected as the representative of the cellular differentiation state. The reason for choosing the dimension with the largest variance is elaborated in section F of supplemental information. For five discrete cell sampling time points (0 and 8 h, and 1, 3, and 7 days) in the EMT dataset, our FatePredictor focuses on the transitional junctions between these time points, aiming to detect potential bifurcation events in cell fate decisions.43 For example, to assess whether a bifurcation occurs between 0 and 8 h, we reconstruct the dynamic cell trajectories of time point 0 h into a pseudotime stage (denoted as pseudotime 0–1) using a dynamic unbalanced optimal transport method. FatePredictor is then applied to determine whether a bifurcation occurs at the endpoint of this stage (pseudotime point 1) and, as shown in Figure 4C, it successfully detects a bifurcation at this junction. Similarly, the dynamic cell trajectories for subsequent time points 8 h and 1, 3, and 7 days are reconstructed as pseudotime stages 1–2, 2–3, 3–4, and 4–5, respectively, to assess whether a bifurcation occurs between the transitions from 8 h to 1 day, 1–3 days, and 3–7 days. The results demonstrate that FatePredictor accurately predicts bifurcations at pseudotime points 2, 3, and 4, corresponding to the respective transitional phases (Figures 4D–4F), in accordance with the observed trajectory of cell differentiation. To further validate the performance of our FatePredictor, we also tested FatePredictor at the midpoints within each pseudotime stage—locations where no bifurcation is expected due to the stable nature of gene expression dynamics (see section G of supplemental information for details). In contrast, as presented in Figures 4C–4F, traditional EWSs including variance and autocorrelation are insufficient for reliably identifying the occurrence of Ts bifurcations, which are classified as a non-catastrophic type. Additionally, our model demonstrates improved accuracy in predicting Ts bifurcation in comparison with existing DL methods (Table 1). Therefore, FatePredictor can accurately identify and distinguish signals of non-catastrophic bifurcations in real-world datasets, effectively addressing the limitations of traditional indicators in detecting such bifurcations.

To further explore both the prediction of cell fate decision-making and the identification of key genes responsible for bifurcation prediction, we applied FatePredictor to a single-cell qPCR data of iPSC differentiation, collected at eight distinct time points.28 The dynamic unbalanced optimal transport method is employed to reconstruct the dynamic trajectories of iPSC differentiation (Figure 5A). In addition, the latent representations obtained from the AE demonstrate a synergistic role and regulatory relationships in promoting cellular proliferation and differentiation, with the dimension with the largest variance AE-2 identified as the key dimension encoding bifurcation information and thus selected as the representative of the iPSC differentiation state (Figure 5B). The inferred temporal trajectory can be partitioned into eight distinct pseudotime stages: pseudotime 0–1 (0 days), pseudotime 1–2 (1 day), pseudotime 2–3 (1.5 days), pseudotime 3–4 (2 days), pseudotime 4–5 (2.5 days), pseudotime 5–6 (3 days), pseudotime 6–7 (4 days), and pseudotime 7–8 (5 days). It can be seen from Figure 5C and Table 1 that FatePredictor can more accurately predict Fold bifurcations at the transition from pseudotime 4–6 (2.5–3 days) to the subsequent pseudotime stages (4 and 5 days) (marked by point 6), compared with existing metrics including DL, variance, autocorrelation, SE, and KC. This predicted result is consistent with findings from the original literature that lineage branching occurs around 3 days during the differentiation of iPSC into cardiomyocytes.28 Moreover, we investigate the impact of in silico gene knockout and overexpression of different highly variable genes (HVGs) on bifurcation predictions, aiming to discover key genes that significantly regulate cell fate decision-making. Specifically, overexpression of five HVGs (see section H of supplemental information) results in a high-probability Pf bifurcation prediction, indicating that increased expression of these genes may enhance the propensity for cellular differentiation (Figure 5D). In contrast, knockout of 25 HVGs, including the 15 previously identified HVGs, yields a prediction confidently categorized as non-bifurcation (Null) (Figures 5E and 5F), suggesting that their reduced expression may impair differentiation potential. Further testing of the Null type is provided in section I of supplemental information. In particular, the selected EPCAM, an epithelial cell adhesion molecule, is identified as playing a role in cell migration, signal transduction, and the regulation of cellular proliferation and differentiation.44 The selected MIXL1 has been implicated in various cellular differentiation processes, including endodermal cell differentiation, hematopoietic progenitor cell differentiation, and the active regulation of mesoderm development.45 Thus, by leveraging expression variations in potential genes, FatePredictor can be employed to pinpoint key genes that are essential in regulating cellular differentiation.

To evaluate FatePredictor on biological dataset with information on natural time-varying series, we use a time-course scRNA-seq data of hESCs transitioning from the pluripotent state through a mesendodermal intermediate to definitive endoderm cells (DECs).27 As illustrated in Figure 6A, the differentiation of hESCs into DECs is divided into five distinct pseudotime stages: pseudotime 0–1 (12 h), pseudotime 1–2 (24 h), and three additional pseudotimes at 36, 72, and 96 h, with a cell fate decision-making occurring at the transition between pseudotime 1–2 (24 h) and the subsequent pseudotime stages, as reported in the original literature. Additionally, the latent representations generated by the AE indicates that AE-1 is the key dimension encoding bifurcation information and is selected as the representative of cellular state transitions. To elucidate the specific mechanisms of cell fate decision-making and identify the associated key genes and pathways, we performed in silico gene knockout and overexpression on HVGs associated with embryonic development (Figure 6B), such as setting the expression levels of the most significant HVGs to zero for the knockout simulations. Specifically, we find that FatePredictor predicts a Pf bifurcation at the transition from pseudotime 1–2 (24 h) to the subsequent pseudotime stages (marked by point 2) before performing in silico gene knockout and overexpression of HVGs (Figure 6C), whereas HVG knockout results in a non-bifurcation (Null) prediction (Figures 6D and 6E). In contrast, the overexpression of HVGs promotes a Pf bifurcation prediction, with the probability of classification as a Pf increasing as the number of overexpressed HVGs rises (Figures 6F–6H), reaching nearly 1 upon the overexpression of 50 HVGs. This finding implies that these HVGs play a key role in regulating cell fate decision-making during hESC differentiation. Particularly, the selected CRHBP has been shown to regulate cellular stress responses and proliferation by modulating CRH activity, which may indirectly affect the differentiation and function of cells essential for embryonic development and tissue regeneration.46
ENTPD3 plays a pivotal role in cellular differentiation bifurcation, serving as a specific marker for the most mature stem cell-derived β cells, thereby underscoring its distinctive function in the transition to cellular maturity.47 Moreover, FatePredictor exhibits superior accuracy in predicting Pf bifurcations compared with other existing methods (Table 1). Consequently, our model can serve as a more effective tool for predicting cell fate decision-making and uncovering key genes and pathways involved in cellular proliferation and differentiation.

Specifically, one of the simulated datasets is derived from a gene regulatory network with two coupled differential equations, while the other is generated from the SERGIO simulator based on stochastic differential equations (refer to section D of supplemental information. The chick heart dataset is derived from experimental observations of spontaneously contracting chick-heart cell clusters, comprising 23 time series with Pd bifurcations and 23 null-time series. Dynamic cell trajectories during epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition for the EMT dataset and during iPSC processes for the iPSC dataset are, respectively, reconstructed using a DL approach based on unbalanced optimal transport theory (see section K of supplemental information for details). The hESC dataset is obtained from a time-course of hESCs transitioning from the pluripotent state through a mesendodermal intermediate to DECs, with information on natural time-varying series. The dimension with the largest variance is chosen as the key dimension to construct the temporal trajectory as it demonstrates better performance in capturing critical transitions and predicting cell fate decisions compared with other dimensions (see section F of supplemental information). The key dimension of the aforementioned datasets was detrended and then used as input for FatePredictor to analyze the dynamic progression of biological systems and predict cell fate decision-making.51
